The paper develops a theory for EM wave scattering by many small particles of arbitrary shape embedded in a homogeneous medium.
Maxwell's system is reduced to a Fredholm second-kind integral equation with weakly singular kernel for single-body scattering.
The many-body problem is solved by deriving linear algebraic systems, completely bypassing integral equations.
The small-body approximation requires ka ≪ 1, where k is the wavenumber and a is the characteristic body size.
The particle distribution is controlled by the formula N(△) = (1/a^(3-κ)) ∫_△ N(x)dx[1+o(1)] with 0 < κ < 1.
The scattering amplitudes V_m and ν_m are computed using formulas (43) and (44) involving integrals of the potential and Green's function.
The approximate solution has error O(a/d + ka) where d is the distance to the nearest particle.
The effective field equation in the limit a→0 is E_e = E_0 + ∫_D g(x,y)C(y)E_e(y)dy with C(x) = c_1m N(x).
The effective refraction coefficient is n²(x) = 1 + k^(-2)C(x), which can be designed arbitrarily.
The limiting effective field does not satisfy ∇·E_e = 0, unlike classical electromagnetic fields.
The term ∇∇·E_e in the limiting equation can be interpreted as a non-classical current or non-local polarization effect.
The total volume of small particles scales as O(a^κ)→0 as a→0, becoming negligible.
The linear algebraic system (49)-(51) is uniquely solvable if condition (53) holds: max_j Σ_m (|a_jm| + |d_jm| + ||B_jm|| + ||C_jm||) < 1.
The potential p(r,a) is chosen as p(r,a) = (γ_m/a^κ)(1-t)²h(t) with ∫p(y)dy = c_1m a^(3-κ).
The asymptotic formulas derived are j_m = c_1m a^(3-κ) and Z_m = (4πκ/3)(∇·E)(x_m)a³ln(a)[1+o(1)].
The paper proves that the only solution to the homogeneous scattering problem satisfying the radiation condition is E = 0.
The Green's function g(x,y) = e^(ik|x-y|)/(4π|x-y|) is used throughout the analysis.
The radiation condition requires ∂v/∂r - ikv = o(1/r) as r→∞, uniformly in all directions.
The method enables creation of materials with desired wave-focusing properties and negative refraction.
The paper extends previous scalar wave scattering theory to the vector electromagnetic case.
The coefficients γ_m in the potential function can be chosen with arbitrary imaginary parts (Im γ_m ≥ 0) to control material properties.
The distance between neighboring particles scales as O(a^(κ/3-1)) as a→0.
The paper provides rigorous mathematical proofs using Fredholm theory and unique continuation principles.
Applications include creating 'smart' materials with designed electromagnetic properties.
The theory applies to particles of arbitrary shape, not just spheres, through the general potential p(x).
